quote.text: Beware of little expenses; a small leak will sink a great ship.
quote.author: Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack

stories.headline: The Deal Is "Very Close." The Toll Booth Is Already Built.
stories.dek: Tehran and Muscat now say a Hormuz corridor is nearly agreed. Read the terms Iran is publishing and it is not a reopening at all: a lane that bars American and Israeli-linked ships, fines violators a fifth of their cargo, and stays shut until Washington pays for an alleged June breach. Six months into the closure, the market has stopped waiting for the strait and started paying to go around it — and Brent, near US$88, is the number doing the talking.

stories.headline: The Screen-Free Craft Where You Don't Own the Result Until It Survives Two Fires
stories.dek: Studio ceramics is clay spun on a powered wheel and braced into shape by hand — and then the hard part, because a pot isn't yours until it lives through a bisque firing and a glaze firing at up to 1,300°C. The hook is a single silent moment; the reality is a two-fire gauntlet, a kiln most apartments can't run, and a boom of mid-career professionals hunting a counterweight to a life lived on screens.

stories.headline: The Man the AI Boom Laid Off Built Korea a Map for the Broke
stories.dek: In March a laid-off Korean developer capped his own food budget at ₩10,000 a day and built a crowdsourced map of every meal cheaper than that. Within a month it had 1.3 million visitors. It is the totem of "jjantech" — thrift reframed as a competitive skill — and the first consumer subculture visibly shaped by white-collar AI displacement. When the FT calls it "Korea's jjantech underclass," it will already have a name, a scoreboard and 2,500 restaurants on it.

stories.headline: A Widening Surplus, and a Fight Over Who It's For
stories.dek: The economy keeps handing the Government room it hasn't spent — Q2 growth at 5.7%, exports up a fifth on the year. So the argument now is not whether Singapore can afford to help stretched households, but how, and whether it should be written into law. The Workers' Party has put its bid on the table early: legislate retrenchment benefits, and account for the surplus. On 23 August the Prime Minister has to answer with a number.

stories.headline: The State Keeps Feeding the Fringe — and That's the Ceiling
stories.dek: Two Confirmed-List sites are on the tender block, one of them a 1,010-unit mega-plot pressed against Bedok MRT. For an owner, the supply story is the quiet one that matters: the Government is keeping the city-fringe pipeline full even as prices split by region, and every future OCR launch is a cap on the last one's upside. The million-dollar-flat record is still setting headlines; the land tenders are setting the price.

stories.headline: Washington Finally Names the Back Door: Renting the Chips It Won't Sell
stories.dek: You can't buy a restricted Nvidia card into China. You can, it turns out, rent one by the hour in Bangkok or Kuala Lumpur — and Chinese AI firms have. This week the US moved on that: the Commerce Department's export arm is drawing up lists of where Blackwell-class compute is being tapped remotely, alongside a House bill to make the rental itself illegal. The catch is that, right now, it isn't.

stories.headline: The 360 We Told You to Wait On Is Here — Keep Waiting a Fortnight
stories.dek: Last issue this desk flagged the Insta360 X6 and said: don't buy until a lab measures it. It went on sale on our cover date, 12 August, at US$699 — a real US$150 jump on the X5. The first hands-on footage is promising. The lab numbers still do not exist. For a buy-once buyer that is the entire verdict, unchanged: it is probably the class leader, and nobody has proven it yet.

stories.headline: The House That Claims It Invented the Chronograph Rings the Bell in Champagne
stories.dek: Louis Moinet marks the 210th anniversary of its founder's Compteur de Tierces — arguably the first true chronograph — with a warm two-tone version of the 1816: an in-house column-wheel chronograph in grade-5 titanium, CHF 28,900. It is the purest buy-once proposition on the desk this week: a genuinely integrated movement at featherweight, from an independent whose whole pitch is that it got there first. The catch is everything a small maker can't offer.

stories.headline: A Reggaetón Superstar Softens, and the Critics' Pick Sneaks Past Her
stories.dek: Two albums landed on 7 August pulling in opposite directions: Karol G's atmospheric heartbreak record, carrying her first-ever Drake collaboration into the pop-blockbuster slot, and Ravyn Lenae's Blue Island, the quieter release the reviewers actually rated highest. It is the recurring culture-desk lesson — the biggest launch and the best-reviewed one are rarely the same record — and, two days out, an album filed at acclaim it hasn't yet had to defend.

stories.kicker: The Family Desk · The Age That Matters
stories.headline: The Screen-Time Rulebook Grew Up — and It Points Straight at Eleven
stories.dek: This year the American Academy of Pediatrics retired its decade-old "hours per day" limit, shifting to what and how over how much. But the newer research adds a sharper edge the headlines miss: the harm signal from social media is not a flat line across childhood. It concentrates in early adolescence, and it runs stronger in girls — which puts an eleven-year-old daughter squarely in the highest-signal window. General guidance, not medical advice.

stories.kicker: The Macro Desk · The Print Nobody's Seen
stories.headline: Oil Wrote the Inflation Scare Before the Data Could
stories.dek: A shut strait and a burning refinery pushed Brent toward US$88, and the bond market did the rest: the ten-year backed up to a one-month high near 4.70% on a higher-for-longer bid. Yet gold ripped through US$4,400 anyway — the tell that this is an inflation scare, not a growth one. The July CPI that settles it prints tonight, Singapore time, after this edition. Nothing constructive here is paid for yet. Market explanation, not investment advice.

stories.headline: Five Minutes a Week, and the "No Time" Excuse Is Officially Dead
stories.dek: A new pooled analysis of "exercise snacks" — bouts of five minutes or less, done a couple of times a day — found they measurably raised VO₂max, at total volumes as low as about four and a half minutes a week. Since VO₂max is one of the strongest predictors of how long you live, that is a real longevity lever hiding in the stairwell. The catch: it helped the previously inactive most, and the number your watch reports is not the number the lab measures. General guidance, not medical advice.

stories.headline: One Ticket to Set an Alarm for This Week, Then an October Crunch
stories.dek: BIGBANG's general sale drops on Thursday — the single act-now item in a Kallang autumn that stacks Post Malone, the Weeknd and Singapore's first-ever F1 Sprint into six weeks. In Japan, September and November carry the sumo and the art, and the family-proof evergreens run all year. Lock the flights and the rooms before the diaries fill.
